content: Pediculosis capitis, commonly known as head lice infestation, is caused by the head louse, Pediculus humanus capitis. This is a type of sucking louse that has evolved to live specifically on the human scalp and neck hairs. Unlike lice found on other parts of the body, such as pubic lice (Pthirus pubis) or body lice (Pediculus humanus humanus), head lice are uniquely adapted to the environment provided by human head hair. Head lice are transmitted primarily through direct head-to-head contact, which is common during activities such as playing sports, spending time on playgrounds, attending camps, or participating in slumber parties. These interactions often occur among children in school or at home. The head louse is an ectoparasite belonging to the order Anoplura, and its only host is humans. It feeds on blood multiple times a day and resides close to the scalp to maintain its body temperature. In the United States, head lice infestations are most frequently observed in preschool and elementary school-aged children, as well as their household members and caregivers. While head lice do not transmit diseases, scratching due to itching can lead to secondary bacterial infections of the skin. Diagnosis History and Symptoms Head lice infestations can sometimes be asymptomatic, particularly during the initial stages or when the infestation is mild. The most common symptom is itching, or pruritus, which results from an allergic reaction to louse bites. Itching may take 4 to 6 weeks to develop after the first infestation. Physical Examination Diagnosis is made by carefully examining the hair and scalp for nits (lice eggs), nymphs (immature lice), or adult lice. Detecting nymphs or adult lice can be challenging, as they are few in number and move quickly to evade detection. If crawling lice are not visible, the presence of nits within 1/4 inch of the scalp confirms an active infestation and necessitates treatment. Other Diagnostic Studies The condition is diagnosed by identifying lice or eggs in the hair, which can be facilitated by using a magnifying glass or running a fine-toothed comb through the hair. In uncertain cases, referral to a healthcare professional may be necessary. However, overdiagnosis is common, with inactive infestations often mistaken for active ones. Consequently, lice-killing treatments are frequently used on children who are not actually infested. The use of a louse comb is the most effective method for detecting live lice. Treatment Secondary Prevention Regular examination of the child’s head using a louse comb allows for early detection of lice infestations. This practice can help identify infestations at an early stage, enabling prompt treatment and reducing the risk of further spread.
